title: Which cuts break a friend network?
hook: Cut the closest friendships or the loosest ones. Which leaves the network in pieces?

knows: strong ties sit inside groups and weak ties between them
doesNotKnow: that removing the weakest links first shatters a network far faster than removing the strongest first

misconception: Cutting the strongest, closest relationships does the most damage to a network.
objective: The learner can explain that links with few shared friends are mostly the bridges between groups, so cutting them first breaks a network into its groups, while cutting close ties inside groups leaves it in one piece.

claims.text: In the stage's networks, cutting the 20% of links with the least overlap leaves a largest group of 10 to 20 of the 60 people; cutting the 20% with the most overlap leaves all 60 in one piece.
claims.source: Builder's own code (makeNet/stateAt in Demo.tsx), re-run in node 2026-10-14 via a transpile-only harness. Model as briefed: 6 groups of 10, each within-group pair linked with probability 0.5, plus 12 distinct random between-group links, mulberry32(seed). Links with equal overlap are cut in a seeded random order (tie key stream mulberry32(seed + 1000)). Cut count = round(share × links). Seed list, chosen by rule: the first five seeds from 1 whose network starts in one piece, i.e. 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 (seeds 2 and 4 skipped because they start disconnected, largest group 50 and 59). The spec's rule also asks that the weak-first 20% cut leaves 30 or fewer; all five meet it, so no seed was skipped for its result. Pinned figures, largest group at 0/10/20/30/40% cut, weakest first | strongest first: seed 1 (149 links) 60/28/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/59; seed 3 (134) 60/56/20/10/10 | 60/60/60/57/55; seed 5 (151) 60/59/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/58; seed 6 (148) 60/30/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/58/58; seed 7 (131) 60/40/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/59/56. Context over seeds 1–500 with the same code: 450 start in one piece; weak-first 20% median 10, 90th percentile 20, maximum 48, 433 of 450 at 30 or fewer; strong-first 20% never below 51. The brief's seed-33 figures came from another generator and are not quoted. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own re-implementation (mulberry32, overlap, seeded tie keys): seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 are the first five that start in one piece; weakest-first 20% leaves 10, 20, 10, 10, 10; strongest-first 20% leaves 60 in all five. Note (non-blocking): the reveal quotes the learner's level when it is 30% or 40% (e.g. seed 3 strongest-first 40% leaves 55); those figures are computed and correct but not in any claim.

claims.text: Link strength = share of friends the two have in common (neighbourhood overlap: shared friends divided by friends of either end, not counting each other).
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (strong and weak ties; neighbourhood overlap). overlap in makeNet, Demo.tsx; a link whose ends have no other friends gets overlap 0. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: The lesson's definition (stage rule text) matches makeNet(): shared neighbours / union of neighbours excluding the two ends. E&K ch. 3 neighbourhood overlap from my knowledge; not opened.

claims.text: Cutting the 20% weakest links first cuts 12 of the 12 between-group links in networks 1, 3, 4 and 5 (seeds 1, 5, 6, 7) and 10 of 12 in network 2 (seed 3); cutting the strongest 20% first cuts none.
claims.source: stateAt(...).bridgesCut in Demo.tsx, builder re-run 2026-10-14, seeds and tie rule as in c1. In the weak-first order the last between-group link sits at rank 30 (seed 1, of 149), 30 (seed 3, of 134; 27 are cut at 20%), 29 (seed 5), 22 (seed 6) and 25 (seed 7). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own run: bridges cut at 20% weakest-first 12, 10, 12, 12, 12 for seeds 1, 3, 5, 6, 7; strongest-first 0 in all.

claims.text: A link with few shared friends usually runs between groups, so cutting those first breaks the network apart; close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (local bridges have neighbourhood overlap 0; weak ties as bridges between tightly knit groups); illustrated on the stage by c1 and c3. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: DISPUTED (direction). Own run of the lesson's networks: bridges almost all have overlap 0 (the max is 0.13), but most links with few shared friends are inside groups: links with overlap 0 are 18/28/29/24/27 in seeds 1/3/5/6/7, of which only 10/10/12/12/12 are bridges, and the weakest 20% (26-30 links) holds 9-12 bridges. So 'a link with few shared friends usually runs between groups' is false here; the converse is true. Fix (builder, reveal and claim): 'Links between groups almost always have few shared friends, so cutting the weakest links first removes them and breaks the network apart. Close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.'

claims.text: The stage's network: 60 people in 6 friend groups of 10, with 12 links between groups.
claims.source: The lesson's model (brief weak-links-hold-it-together, company/domains/briefs/probability.chance.md, Course: NCM); a toy model, not data about a real network. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: GROUPS 6 x SIZE 10, BRIDGES 12 distinct between-group links in makeNet(); predict text '60 people, 6 friend groups'.

recall.question: A company wants to keep its teams talking. Which relationships, if lost, would split it into isolated teams fastest?
options: The closest friendships inside each team
The loose acquaintances between teams who share few contacts
It makes no difference which go
recall.why: Links with few shared contacts are usually the bridges between groups. Lose them and the teams fall apart; close ties sit inside teams, which stay connected through each other without them.
